Photo location guide

Add Location to Camera Photos in Apple Photos

For a few photos at a known place, start with Apple Photos. For a trip with many stops, use capture times and location evidence to suggest a different place for each photo.

Updated November 4, 2026

Start with one photo, not the whole tripAdd a known place with the built-in toolsCopy a location when the photos share one spotCheck time zones and the camera clockBatch-fill a trip using same-trip iPhone photosCheck the saved result and any exported copy

Start with one photo, not the whole trip

Open an imported camera photo in Apple Photos and look at its information. On iPhone, swipe up or tap Info. On Mac, select it and press Command-I. Check the capture date, camera details and map. If no location is listed, the photo needs coordinates before it can appear on the map. A filename, album name or recognizable landmark is not a saved GPS location.

Importing a photo moves the image into your library; it cannot reconstruct a position the camera never recorded. Keep the camera card or another backup while you organize the trip. If the photos are still on the card, follow the camera import guide first.

Add a known place with the built-in tools

  1. On iPhone, open the photo’s information and use Add a location, or Adjust beside an existing place.
  2. Search for the place where you took it and select the appropriate result. Check nearby places with similar names before accepting.
  3. For photos from the same spot, select that small group in the library and use the More menu’s Adjust Location action. Some versions put it under Adjust Info.
  4. Reopen an individual photo and check its map. A group selection is useful only when every selected image belongs at the same place.

These are Apple’s location adjustment tools. If you know only the town, an approximate town location can help you organize photos, but it does not establish an exact shooting position. Avoid giving a whole day the location of its first stop.

Copy a location when the photos share one spot

On Mac, select a photo with the correct place. Choose Image > Location > Copy Location, select the target photos, then choose Image > Location > Assign Location. Apple documents this in its Mac metadata guide. This copies one location; it does not follow your route or match each photo by time. Check the selection before applying it, especially if it contains photos that already have locations.

Check time zones and the camera clock

Before trying time matching, compare a camera photo with an iPhone photo of the same moment. A camera left on home time can be several hours away from local time. A clock that simply runs slow can be a few minutes out. Both can send a plausible-looking suggestion to the wrong part of the day.

Use a recognizable moment, such as a shared view at a station, to judge the difference. Verify another moment later in the trip. If you changed the camera clock halfway through, treat the two periods separately. Do the same for different cameras: their clock errors need not be identical. See the GPX and clock-offset guide for the track-based workflow.

Batch-fill a trip using same-trip iPhone photos

LensPin is a batch option when the camera photos are already in Apple Photos and you have geotagged iPhone photos from the same trip. It matches capture times against those reference photos. Geotagged photos from other cameras, GPX tracks and Apple Health/Fitness workout routes can also provide location evidence. Journeys are grouped automatically.

  1. Choose a manageable set of camera photos without locations, starting with one trip and one camera clock.
  2. Use same-trip geotagged photos as the source. Confirm that your reference photos actually show the right places.
  3. If the clocks differ, preview the camera clock offset. This changes the matching preview, not the photos’ capture dates.
  4. Review every suggestion before saving. Skip places that the available evidence cannot support, particularly around long gaps or fast travel.

A phone photo taken at lunch does not prove where you were hours later. More reference points can make the trip easier to check, but no matching method can recover a precise place from missing evidence. LensPin processes on device, never overwrites existing locations and does not import from cameras or record GPX.

Check the saved result and any exported copy

After saving, return to Apple Photos and inspect the map for the first, middle and last parts of the batch, plus any uncertain suggestions. If a photo has a location but seems absent from the map, use the map troubleshooting guide. Brand-specific checks are collected in camera photos with no location.

LensPin saves locations to the Apple Photos library, not the original files. If you need a separate file containing GPS in EXIF, export a JPG copy with Include location enabled. Inspect that copy before sharing it; you may prefer to omit a private location.

LensPin is a free download for iPhone/iPad with iOS/iPadOS 17+ and native Mac with macOS 14+. The first 100 successful location additions are free; optional Unlimited is a one-time purchase (US $3.99 / CN ¥12). For desktop steps, see adding photo locations on Mac.
